title: The Brothers of Jesus
lead: The Gospels name four brothers of Jesus, James, Joseph (Joses), Simon and Judas, and mention sisters. They did not believe in him at first, but after the resurrection they were among the church's leaders.

sections.b: "Isn't this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James, Joses, Judas and Simon? Aren't his sisters here with us?" (Mark 6:3; Matthew 13:55–56). During his ministry "not even his brothers were putting their faith in him" (John 7:5). After the resurrection they were praying with the apostles (Acts 1:14). The risen Jesus appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), who led the Jerusalem church (Acts 15:13; Galatians 1:19). Paul says "the brothers of the Lord" traveled with their wives (1 Corinthians 9:5).
sections.refs: Mark 3:31–35; Mark 6:3; Matthew 13:55–56; John 7:3–5; Acts 1:14; Acts 15:13; 1 Corinthians 9:5; 1 Corinthians 15:7; Galatians 1:19

sections.b: Three views. Helvidius (380s): younger children of Mary and Joseph, the view of most Protestants today. Joseph's sons by an earlier marriage: this appears by about AD 150 in the Protevangelium of James, is assumed by Origen, and was championed by Epiphanius; it is the Eastern Orthodox view. Cousins: argued by Jerome against Helvidius in the 380s, and the usual Roman Catholic view, since Hebrew and Aramaic used "brother" broadly. The Greek adelphos normally means a brother, but can be wider. The second and third views are tied to the belief that Mary remained a virgin.
